literary_identity: Physician, antiquary, and prose stylist; author of Religio Medici (1643), Hydriotaphia (Urn Burial, 1658), and The Garden of Cyrus (1658), whose majestic, digressive, Latinate prose is among the richest in English and fuses faith, scepticism, and learned curiosity.
biography: Born 19 October 1605 in London, educated at Winchester and Pembroke College, Oxford (BA 1626, MA 1629), then studying medicine at Montpellier, Padua, and Leiden (MD 1633). He settled as a physician in Norwich (1637), where he lived for the rest of his life, marrying Dorothy Mileham (1641) and fathering twelve children. Religio Medici, circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent (1643), made his name; he answered critics and published Pseudodoxia Epidemica (1646–72), a vast enquiry into 'vulgar errors', and the twin treatises Hydriotaphia and The Garden of Cyrus (1658). Knighted by Charles II in 1671, he corresponded with the Royal Society and died on 19 October 1682.
literary_profile: The physician-essayist who meditated on belief, death, and the wonders of the natural world in a grand, allusive prose, holding faith and sceptical enquiry in a richly personal balance.
stylistic_characteristics: Sonorous, Latinate, digressive prose; paradox and learned allusion; a baroque richness of phrase; antiquarian and scientific curiosity; and a meditative, tolerant tone.
intellectual_concerns: Faith and reason; death, burial, and the resurrection; the errors of popular belief; nature, plants, and antiquities; the mystery of the self; and Christian tolerance.
historical_significance: Browne is one of the supreme English prose stylists, influencing Johnson, De Quincey, Lamb, and Woolf; Religio Medici created a new genre of personal, tolerant religious autobiography, and Urn Burial remains a masterpiece of meditative antiquarianism.
biographical_uncertainty: Browne's life is well documented through his letters and Norwich records; the publication history of Religio Medici (pirated editions before his authorised text) is complex.

literary_identity: Anglican biographer and author of The Compleat Angler (1653), the beloved pastoral dialogue of fishing whose serene celebration of the contemplative country life made it one of the most reprinted books in English.
biography: Born 9 August 1593 at Stafford; apprenticed to a linen-draper, he prospered as a haberdasher in London (Fleet Street and later Chancery Lane) and moved in literary circles. A devout royalist Anglican, he served the cause during the Civil Wars and at the Restoration. He wrote gentle biographies of John Donne (1640), Sir Henry Wotton, Richard Hooker, George Herbert (1670), and Robert Sanderson, collected as Walton's Lives. His masterpiece The Compleat Angler (1653), enlarged over five editions to 1676 (with Charles Cotton's second part on fly-fishing), became a classic. He retired to the country and died on 15 December 1683 at Winchester, aged 90.
literary_profile: The biographer of the devout and the angler of the contemplative life, whose unhurried, genial prose celebrates friendship, piety, and the pleasures of riverside retirement.
stylistic_characteristics: Gentle, pastoral, conversational prose; dialogue form (Piscator, Venator, Auceps); a serene, pious tone; digressive quotation of verse and lore; and unpretentious charm.
intellectual_concerns: The contemplative and retired life; friendship and piety; the natural world of rivers and fish; Anglican devotion and modest virtue; and the celebration of simple pleasures.
historical_significance: The Compleat Angler has been continuously in print and is one of the most beloved of English books; Walton's Lives established a tradition of affectionate biographical portraiture and shaped the ideal of the Anglican 'holy life'.
biographical_uncertainty: Walton's life is documented; his Lives blend fact with hagiographic affection and are not always reliable as biography, and his dates for some subjects are traditional.

literary_identity: Anglican divine and devotional writer, called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'; his Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651) are the supreme prose achievements of Caroline Anglican piety, rich in imagery, learning, and moral casuistry.
biography: Born August 1613 at Cambridge, son of a barber; educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (BA 1630, MA 1634) and All Souls, Oxford. Patronised by William Laud and Charles I, he became a royalist chaplain, was twice imprisoned during the Civil Wars, and was deprived of his living. In seclusion in Wales he wrote his great devotional manuals Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651), and the casuistical Ductor Dubitantium (1660). At the Restoration he was consecrated Bishop of Down and Connor (1661) and Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College, Dublin; he died on 13 August 1667 at Lisburn.
literary_profile: The eloquent Caroline divine whose devotional prose combines baroque imagery, immense learning, and tender moral guidance, treating the whole of life as a preparation for a holy death.
stylistic_characteristics: Lush, metaphorical, Latinate prose; abundant simile and classical and scriptural allusion; casuistical moral reasoning; and a rich, musical rhythm.
intellectual_concerns: Holy living and dying; Christian virtue, patience, and repentance; liberty of conscience and toleration (The Liberty of Prophesying, 1647); moral casuistry; and Anglican devotion.
historical_significance: Holy Living and Holy Dying shaped English devotional prose and the Anglican ideal of the good life and good death for centuries; Taylor's eloquence and advocacy of toleration mark him as one of the greatest prose writers and most liberal-minded of the Caroline divines.
biographical_uncertainty: Taylor's life is documented; his imprisoned royalist years and some details of his preferment rest on tradition and ecclesiastical records.

literary_identity: Puritan preacher, nonconformist, and author of The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, 1684), the greatest allegory in English and one of the most widely read books ever written, born of his years of imprisonment for preaching without a licence.
biography: Born November 1628 (baptised 30 November) at Elstow, Bedfordshire, son of a tinker; little educated, he served briefly in the Parliamentary army and followed his father's trade. After a profound spiritual crisis recounted in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666), he became a Baptist preacher at Bedford. Refusing to conform after the Restoration, he was imprisoned for twelve years (1660–72) and briefly again in 1675–76, during which he wrote and, likely, began The Pilgrim's Progress. Published in two parts (1678, 1684), it was an immediate and enduring popular success. He also wrote The Holy War (1682), The Life and Death of Mr Badman (1680), and much doctrinal and controversial prose. He died on 31 August 1688 in London after a stormy journey.
literary_profile: The tinker-preacher whose plain, biblical, vividly imaginative prose gave the Puritan pilgrimage of the soul an unforgettable narrative form, drawing its power from scripture, the vernacular, and his own tormented and triumphant experience.
stylistic_characteristics: Allegory with concrete, homely, scriptural imagery; a plain, vigorous, rhythmic prose saturated with the Bible; vivid personification (Christian, Faithful, Apollyon, Mr Worldly Wiseman); and dream-frame narrative.
intellectual_concerns: Salvation, grace, and the pilgrim's journey; sin, despair, and assurance; the Christian life as warfare and pilgrimage; persecution and nonconformity; and the vanity of the world.
historical_significance: The Pilgrim's Progress is the supreme English allegory and a foundational text of Protestant spirituality, translated into hundreds of languages and influencing the novel, hymnody, and countless writers from Dickens to the present; Grace Abounding is a landmark of spiritual autobiography.
biographical_uncertainty: Bunyan's life is documented through his own writings and Bedford church records; the exact circumstances and dates of his composition of The Pilgrim's Progress during imprisonment are traditional rather than certain.

literary_identity: Anglican clergyman, historian, and wit; author of The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), a compendium of characters and maxims, and The History of the Worthies of England (1662), a pioneering biographical-topographical survey written in an energetic, proverbial style.
biography: Born 1608 at Aldwincle, Northamptonshire (the same parish as Dryden); a prodigy educated at Queens' College, Cambridge (BA 1624/25) and Sidney Sussex College. He held various livings, served as a royalist chaplain during the Civil Wars, and was known for his preaching, memory, and wit. His major works include The Holy State (1642), Good Thoughts in Bad Times (1645), The Church-History of Britain (1655), and the posthumous Worthies of England (1662). A moderate during the Interregnum, he was restored at the Restoration and died on 16 August 1661 in London.
literary_profile: The learned, witty compiler and historian whose pithy, proverbial, digressive style and love of anecdotes and characters made him one of the most readable prose writers of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: Terse, epigrammatic, proverbial prose; the 'character' sketch; abundant anecdote, pun, and quotation; a genial, learned wit; and a digressive, associative method.
intellectual_concerns: Moral and religious instruction; English history, biography, and topography; the virtues of the 'holy state' and the vices of the 'profane'; wit and wisdom; and moderation in the church.
historical_significance: Fuller's Worthies is a foundational work of English local history and biography, and his Church-History a pioneering ecclesiastical history; his prose style, full of quotable maxims, was widely admired and influential.
biographical_uncertainty: Fuller's life is documented; the accuracy of some of his historical and biographical anecdotes was questioned even in his day and he himself admitted a love of a good story.

literary_identity: Antiquary, biographer, and gossip-collector; his Brief Lives — vivid, candid, anecdotal sketches of his famous contemporaries (Shakespeare, Hobbes, Donne, Bacon) — invented an intimate, factual mode of biography and preserved priceless literary history.
biography: Born 12 March 1626 at Easton Piers, Wiltshire; educated at Trinity College, Oxford (no degree) and the Middle Temple. A gentleman antiquary and Fellow of the Royal Society (1663), he roamed the country recording monuments, folklore (Remains of Gentilisme and Judaisme), and the lives and sayings of learned men. A close friend of Hobbes (whose Life he wrote), he compiled his 'Minutes of Lives' — the Brief Lives — mostly in the 1660s–90s, not intended for publication. Ruined by lawsuits, he lived on others' charity and died in Oxford on 7 June 1697. His manuscripts, held by the Bodleian, were published in full only in the twentieth century.
literary_profile: The pioneer of intimate, empirical biography, whose frank, discursive, note-strewn 'Lives' capture the personalities, quirks, and scandals of the great with an unprecedented immediacy.
stylistic_characteristics: Anecdotal, colloquial, note-form prose; candid reportage and quotation of others' testimony; digressive and unfinished quality; and an antiquarian accumulation of fact and folklore.
intellectual_concerns: Biography and personal character; antiquities, monuments, and folklore; the lives of the learned and of Hobbes; astrology and the supernatural; and the preservation of literary history.
historical_significance: Brief Lives is a unique and indispensable source for seventeenth-century literary and intellectual history and a founding work of modern, personal biography; Aubrey's methods anticipated the empirical, factual approach of later biographers.
biographical_uncertainty: Aubrey's own life is documented through his manuscripts and correspondents; his Brief Lives are notes and gossip of varying reliability, requiring editorial caution.

literary_identity: Letter-writer; her Letters to Sir William Temple (1652–54), written during their protracted courtship against her family's opposition, are among the finest and most natural prose works of the century and a rare surviving woman's voice of the Interregnum.
biography: Born 1627 at Chicksands Priory, Bedfordshire, daughter of a royalist family; she nursed her father during the Civil Wars and lost most of her siblings. Between 1652 and 1654 she conducted a secret correspondence with William Temple (later the diplomat and essayist), whom she married in 1654 against strong family pressure and other suitors. Her letters — witty, tender, shrewd, and critical of the romances and poetry of the day — survive in some seventy-seven; Temple preserved them and they were published in 1888. She lived as Lady Temple, accompanying her husband's career, and died in 1695.
literary_profile: The natural, intelligent letter-writer whose prose, free of artifice, offers a woman's candid view of love, family duty, books, and society in the 1650s, and a remarkable literary self-portrait.
stylistic_characteristics: Easy, colloquial, unforced prose; wit and psychological insight; literary criticism and quotation; and an intimate epistolary voice of great spontaneity.
intellectual_concerns: Love, marriage, and family obligation; the position and intelligence of women; reading, romances, and poetry; society and character; and the conduct of the inner life.
historical_significance: Osborne's Letters are a masterpiece of informal English prose and one of the most important documents by a seventeenth-century woman, valued for their literary quality and as a witness to women's intellectual life and to the early career of Temple.
biographical_uncertainty: Only Osborne's side of the correspondence survives in full; her later life is documented mainly through Temple's papers, and the letters' publication was long delayed.

literary_identity: Diplomat, statesman, and essayist; author of Observations upon the United Provinces (1673) and the elegant miscellaneous essays Of Gardens (1685) and Of Poetry, whose polished, urbane prose and patronage of Swift made him a central figure of late-century letters.
biography: Born 25 April 1628 in London, son of Sir John Temple; educated at Bishop's Stortford and Emmanuel College, Cambridge (under Ralph Cudworth), travelling widely in Europe. He served as ambassador and negotiator (the Triple Alliance, 1668; the treaties of Nijmegen), and as Secretary of State (1679), before retiring to Moor Park, Surrey. There he wrote his Observations upon the United Provinces (1673), his Miscellanea (1680, 1690), and essays including 'Upon the Gardens of Epicurus' (1685), and employed the young Jonathan Swift as his secretary (1689–99). His 'Essay upon the Ancient and Modern Learning' (1690) provoked the Battle of the Books. He died on 27 January 1699.
literary_profile: The cultivated statesman-essayist whose clear, graceful, conversational prose exemplifies the polite ideal of the late seventeenth century and who introduced the Chinese garden and a cosmopolitan urbane taste to English letters.
stylistic_characteristics: Polished, lucid, urbane prose; the short, balanced sentence; conversational ease; digressive reflection; and a Horatian ideal of retirement.
intellectual_concerns: Politics, diplomacy, and the Dutch republic; gardens, retirement, and the Epicurean ideal; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; poetry and wit; and the conduct of public and private life.
historical_significance: Temple's essays shaped Augustan prose style and the taste for retirement and gardening; his patronage launched Swift, and his 'Ancient and Modern Learning' essay ignited the Battle of the Books that Swift and Wotton fought out.
biographical_uncertainty: Temple's diplomatic career is well documented in state papers; his private life and the details of his relationship with Swift and his household are known through correspondence and memoirs.

literary_identity: Naval administrator and diarist; his Diary (1660–69), kept in shorthand and published only in the nineteenth century, is the most famous diary in English — a candid, vivid record of the Restoration, the Great Plague, and the Great Fire, and of his own private life.
biography: Born 23 February 1633 in Salisbury Court, London, educated at St Paul's School and Magdalene College, Cambridge (BA 1654). Through the patronage of his cousin Edward Montagu (later Earl of Sandwich) he entered the Navy Office as Clerk of the Acts (1660), becoming an able administrator and later Secretary to the Admiralty. From January 1660 to May 1669 he kept a meticulous private diary in shorthand covering public affairs (the coronation, the Dutch Wars, the Plague of 1665, the Fire of 1666) and his own finances, ambitions, affairs, and domestic life. Failing eyesight ended the diary in 1669; he served as MP and President of the Royal Society (1684–86) but lost office after the Revolution. He died on 26 May 1703.
literary_profile: The incomparable diarist whose immediacy, curiosity, and unembarrassed self-revelation — of work, pleasure, money, sex, music, and public catastrophe — create an unrivalled portrait of Restoration England and of a single vivid personality.
stylistic_characteristics: Spontaneous, detailed, colloquial prose in shorthand; a diary's day-by-day immediacy; candid self-scrutiny; vivid reportage of events; and an eye for the telling particular.
intellectual_concerns: Public affairs and naval administration; ambition, money, and social climbing; pleasure, music, theatre, and women; the Plague and the Fire; and the private conscience.
historical_significance: The Diary is a primary historical source of the first importance for the 1660s and a literary classic; its frankness and observational brilliance established the diary as a major form and Pepys as one of the most beloved figures in English letters.
major_influences: (private, non-literary: his own experience and public office)
biographical_uncertainty: Pepys's Diary and letters are richly documented; the diary was deciphered only in the nineteenth century, and some shorthand passages remain uncertain in reading.

literary_identity: Diarist, author, horticulturist, and founding Fellow of the Royal Society; his long Diary (1641–1706) records the intellectual and public life of the age, and his Sylva (1664) — a plea for reforestation — was a pioneering work of natural history and one of the Society's first publications.
biography: Born 31 October 1620 at Wotton, Surrey, educated at Balliol College, Oxford and the Middle Temple. He travelled Europe (1643–52), keeping a journal, and after the Restoration settled at Sayes Court, Deptford. A founder-member of the Royal Society (1662), he published Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees (1664), Fumifugium (1661, on air pollution), and works on engraving, numismatics, and horticulture, and translated Lucretius and others. His Diary, kept over six decades, is the great public counterpart to Pepys's private one. A devout Anglican and royalist, he died on 27 February 1706.
literary_profile: The cultivated gentleman-scholar and improver whose wide-ranging diary, essays, and horticultural writings document the new science, the arts, and public affairs with learned, pious, and practical curiosity.
stylistic_characteristics: Learned, observant, sometimes formal prose; the discursive diary and treatise; antiquarian and scientific detail; and a pious, improving tone.
intellectual_concerns: Horticulture, forestry, and the improvement of the land; the new science and the Royal Society; art, architecture, and engraving; air pollution and the environment; religion and public affairs.
historical_significance: Sylva is a landmark of natural history and environmental writing and helped reforest England for the navy; Evelyn's Diary is an invaluable record of the intellectual and cultural life of the seventeenth century, complementing Pepys.
biographical_uncertainty: Evelyn's life and writings are thoroughly documented through his diary, letters, and family papers; his works are numerous and some are translations.

literary_identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of Leviathan (1649), the founding text of modern political philosophy, whose materialist, mechanistic system and prose of austere clarity transformed English thought and letters.
biography: Born 5 April 1588 at Westport, Wiltshire (the year of the Armada — 'fear and I were born twins', he joked); educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served for decades as tutor and secretary to the Cavendish family (Earls of Devonshire), travelling Europe and meeting Mersenne, Gassendi, Descartes, and Galileo. Alarmed by the political crisis, he went into exile in Paris (1640–51), publishing De Cive (1642) and, in 1651, Leviathan, whose defence of absolute sovereignty and its Erastianism offended both royalists and Parliamentarians. He returned to England, was distrusted by the restored court, and, after the Clarendon attack and the 1666 parliamentary scrutiny of 'atheism', published little more political philosophy. His later works include Behemoth (1668–70) and an autobiography in verse. He died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick.
literary_profile: The philosopher who derived the state from a contract among self-interested individuals in a 'war of every man against every man', and who wrote with a logical, powerful, and lucid prose that made philosophy English literature.
stylistic_characteristics: Rigorous, deductive argument; a clear, forceful, sometimes ironic prose; striking metaphors (the state as 'Leviathan', life as 'nasty, brutish, and short'); and a materialist, mechanistic vocabulary.
intellectual_concerns: Sovereignty, the social contract, and the state of nature; materialism and mechanism; human nature, appetite, and reason; religion and its political control; and the philosophy of language and knowledge.
historical_significance: Leviathan founded modern political philosophy and social contract theory, profoundly influencing Locke, Rousseau, and all subsequent thought; Hobbes's materialism and prose style also made him a central, if feared, figure in English intellectual and literary history.
biographical_uncertainty: Hobbes's life is well documented (including his own prose and verse autobiographies and Aubrey's Life); the sincerity of his religious professions remains debated.

literary_identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), the foundational text of British empiricism, and the Two Treatises of Government (1689), whose defence of natural rights, consent, and toleration shaped the Enlightenment and modern liberalism.
biography: Born 29 August 1632 at Wrington, Somerset, educated at Westminster and Christ Church, Oxford, where he turned from scholasticism to medicine and the new science, associating with Boyle and Sydenham and joining the Royal Society (1668). He became physician and close adviser to Anthony Ashley Cooper (later Earl of Shaftesbury), was drawn into Whig politics and the Exclusion Crisis, and fled to Holland (1683–89). Returning with William of Orange after the Revolution, he published in 1689 the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the Two Treatises of Government, and A Letter Concerning Toleration, and later Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693) and The Reasonableness of Christianity (1695). He spent his last years at Oates in Essex in the Masham household, dying on 28 October 1704.
literary_profile: The empiricist who argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate furnished only by experience, and the liberal who grounded government in consent, natural rights, and the pursuit of happiness — a prose of patient, plain, argumentative clarity.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, methodical, argumentative prose; plain style as an ideal; careful definition and example; and a moderate, reasonable, conversational tone addressed to the 'underlabourer's' task.
intellectual_concerns: Knowledge, ideas, and empiricism; personal identity and the limits of understanding; natural rights, consent, and government; religious toleration; property and money; and education.
historical_significance: Locke founded British empiricism and modern liberal political theory, profoundly influencing Berkeley, Hume, the American and French revolutions, and all subsequent Western political thought; his Essays and Treatises are also classics of English prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Locke's life is thoroughly documented through his correspondence and journals; the authorship of the Two Treatises (published anonymously) was long uncertain but is now securely his.

literary_identity: Natural philosopher and chemist, a founder of the Royal Society; his The Sceptical Chymist (1661) championed the new experimental method and corpuscular philosophy, and his pious writings defended Christianity as compatible with science.
biography: Born 25 January 1627 at Lismore Castle, County Waterford, the youngest son of Richard Boyle, first Earl of Cork (the richest man in Britain); educated at Eton and in Europe (Geneva, Florence, where he read Galileo). Settling in England, he joined the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society (chartered 1662), conducted experiments with his assistant Robert Hooke (inventor of the air pump), and formulated Boyle's law of gases. A devout Anglican, he wrote prolifically on both science and religion — The Sceptical Chymist (1661), Some Physico-Theological Considerations (1665), and works defending the faith — and endowed the Boyle Lectures. He died on 31 December 1691.
literary_profile: The experimental philosopher who separated chemistry from alchemy and medicine, argued for the corpuscular (mechanical) philosophy, and reconciled scientific enquiry with Christian piety in a clear, plain prose.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, experimental, methodical prose; detailed reports of apparatus and results; dialogic form (The Sceptical Chymist); and a pious, reasoned apologetic style.
intellectual_concerns: Experimental method and the corpuscular philosophy; chemistry, gases, and the air pump; the reconciliation of science and religion; the plain style of the new science; and natural theology.
historical_significance: Boyle is a founder of modern chemistry and of the experimental method, and his advocacy of the plain style and of physico-theology shaped both scientific writing and the religious defence of science; the Boyle Lectures continued his apologetic project for generations.
biographical_uncertainty: Boyle's life and works are thoroughly documented; his scientific and religious writings are extensive and partly published posthumously.

literary_identity: Prolific and original author of philosophy, science, poetry, drama, and prose fiction; the first woman to write science fiction (The Description of a New World, Called The Blazing World, 1666) and the first woman admitted to a meeting of the Royal Society (1667).
biography: Born c. 1623 at Colchester, daughter of Sir Charles Lucas; she became a maid of honour to Queen Henrietta Maria and followed her into exile in Paris (1644), where she married William Cavendish, Marquis (later Duke) of Newcastle. She published prolifically from 1653 — Poems and Fancies, Philosophical Fancies, Orations, plays, and The Blazing World (1666), appended to her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (a critique of the Royal Society and of Hooke's microscopy). Eccentric, ambitious, and ridiculed as 'Mad Madge', she nevertheless defended women's education and imagination and visited the Royal Society in 1667. She died on 15 December 1673 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The bold, self-taught natural philosopher and imaginative writer who, across genres, developed a vitalist materialism and gave it narrative form in a utopian romance, while asserting a woman's right to knowledge and fame.
stylistic_characteristics: Speculative, energetic, sometimes digressive prose and verse; philosophical dialogue and treatise; utopian romance and imaginary voyage; and a defiantly personal, self-promoting voice.
intellectual_concerns: Natural philosophy and vitalist materialism; the critique of mechanism and the microscope; women's education, authorship, and fame; utopia and imaginary worlds; and the relation of fancy and reason.
historical_significance: Cavendish is a pioneering woman of letters and of science, an early critic of the new experimental philosophy, and the author of the first English science-fiction narrative; feminist and history-of-science scholarship has restored her as a major, original figure.
biographical_uncertainty: Cavendish's life is documented through her own (self-dramatising) memoirs and her husband's biography; her birth year is approximate and her reception was distorted by contemporary mockery.

literary_identity: Philosopher; her posthumous The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy (1690, Latin 1692) advanced an original metaphysical monism of living spirit and influenced Henry More, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and later thinkers.
biography: Born 14 December 1631 in London, daughter of Sir Heneage Finch; she was educated at home, corresponded in philosophy with Henry More (her brother's Cambridge tutor) from her teens, and married Edward Conway (later Viscount and Earl of Conway) in 1651. Suffering lifelong, disabling headaches, she sought cures across Europe, and in her later years was drawn to Quakerism (she received Quaker visitors including George Fox's circle). She wrote her philosophical treatise in the 1670s; it was published posthumously in Amsterdam (1690, English; 1692, Latin) and circulated among European philosophers. She died on 18 February 1679.
literary_profile: The original metaphysician who argued against the dualism of Descartes and the materialism of Hobbes for a universe of spiritual, mutable substance, anticipating Leibniz's monads in a work admired across Europe.
stylistic_characteristics: Systematic philosophical argument; a treatise of propositions and demonstrations; metaphysical reasoning about substance, spirit, and creation; and a clear, technical prose.
intellectual_concerns: The nature of substance, spirit, and body; the critique of Descartes and Hobbes; the goodness and unity of creation; free will and theodicy; and religion and philosophy.
historical_significance: Conway's Principles is a major, original work of early modern philosophy by a woman, influencing the Cambridge Platonists and Leibniz, and her recovery has established her as a significant figure in the history of philosophy.
biographical_uncertainty: Conway's life is documented through letters and family records; her single major work was published posthumously and its reception history is partly reconstructed.

literary_identity: Philosopher, polemicist, and early feminist; her A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (1694, 1697) argued for a women's educational institution and her Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700) exposed the double standard, making her a founder of English feminist argument.
biography: Born 12 November 1666 at Newcastle upon Tyne, daughter of a coal merchant; deprived of formal education and a dowry by her father's early death, she moved to London (c. 1688) and, supported by a circle of aristocratic women patrons, became a prolific writer. A High Church Tory and intellectual correspondent of John Norris and George Hickes, she published A Serious Proposal to the Ladies (Part I 1694, Part II 1697), advocating a Protestant 'monastery' or academy for women's education, and Some Reflections upon Marriage (1700). She also wrote philosophical and theological works (The Christian Religion, 1705) and controversial pamphlets, and ran a charity school for girls in Chelsea in retirement. She died on 9 May 1731.
literary_profile: The rigorous female philosopher and polemicist who used Cartesian method and High Church theology to argue that women are rational souls entitled to education and to critique the inequalities of marriage and custom.
stylistic_characteristics: Argumentative, ironic, and polemical prose; rhetorical questions and wit; philosophical reasoning applied to women's condition; and an earnest, hortatory tone.
intellectual_concerns: Women's education and rational capacity; marriage and the double standard; female friendship and community; religion and reason; and political and theological controversy.
historical_significance: Astell is a pioneering English feminist philosopher whose proposals for women's education and her critique of marriage anticipate later feminist thought; her recovery has made her central to the history of women's writing and of the Enlightenment debate on women.
biographical_uncertainty: Astell's life is documented through her works, correspondence, and patrons; details of her early life and her Chelsea charity school rest on records and tradition.

literary_identity: Latitudinarian clergyman, philosopher, and apologist for the new science; his Scepsis Scientifica (1665) argued a constructive scepticism and the value of experimental enquiry, and his writings on witchcraft defended the reality of spirits against atheism.
biography: Born c. 1636 at Plymouth, educated at Exeter College and Lincoln College, Oxford (MA 1658), where he came under the influence of the Platonic and latitudinarian circle. A Fellow of the Royal Society (1664), he published The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), revised as Scepsis Scientifica (1665), advocating a modest, probabilist scepticism and the new experimental philosophy, and Essays on Several Important Subjects (1670). As a clergyman (vicar of Frome and later a prebendary of Worcester) he wrote latitudinarian sermons and, famously, defended belief in witchcraft and spirits (Saducismus Triumphatus, 1681, posthumous) as a bulwark against atheism. He died on 4 November 1680.
literary_profile: The 'sceptical' apologist who turned doubt to the service of the new science and of religion, arguing for a plain, probabilist, experimental approach to knowledge in an influential, readable prose.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, persuasive, latitudinarian prose; philosophical scepticism turned constructive; advocacy of the Royal Society's plain style; and a reasoned, moderate argumentative manner.
intellectual_concerns: Scepticism and the limits of dogmatism; the new experimental philosophy; the defence of religion and of spirits against atheism; the reform of prose style; and religious toleration and latitude.
historical_significance: Glanvill was a leading populariser of the Royal Society's ideals and of latitudinarian theology; his Scepsis Scientifica influenced Locke and the plain-style movement, and his witchcraft writings reflect the period's contested boundary between science and superstition.
biographical_uncertainty: Glanvill's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through his works and Royal Society records; his witchcraft defence has been much debated by historians.

literary_identity: Clergyman, natural philosopher, and organizer of science; the central figure of the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society, whose works on a universal philosophical language and on the plurality of worlds made him a pioneer of scientific communication.
biography: Born 1614 (baptised 1 January 1614/15), probably at Fawsley, Northamptonshire; educated at New Inn Hall and Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as chaplain and, under the Commonwealth, as Warden of Wadham College, Oxford (1648), where he gathered the circle of experimental philosophers (including Boyle, Wren, and Hooke) that formed the nucleus of the Royal Society. He married Robina, sister of Oliver Cromwell (1656), was deprived at the Restoration but reconciled, became vicar of Polebrook and then Dean of Exeter. His works include The Discovery of a World in the Moone (1638) and An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (1668), a scheme for a universal language. He died on 19 November 1672.
literary_profile: The genial organizer and populariser of the new science, whose speculative works on the moon, cryptography, and a philosophical 'real character' promoted experimental learning and clear communication.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, expository, speculative prose; scientific and linguistic schemes; popularisation of the new philosophy; and an irenic, moderate clerical tone.
intellectual_concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institutions; a universal philosophical language; the plurality of worlds and astronomy; cryptography and communication; and religious latitude and toleration.
historical_significance: Wilkins was the practical founder of the Royal Society's collaborative ethos and a pioneer of the search for a universal language and of scientific popularisation; his Essay influenced later philosophers of language and utopian writers.
biographical_uncertainty: Wilkins's birthplace and early life are uncertain; his career is documented through university, church, and Royal Society records.

literary_identity: Clergyman, poet, and historian of science; his History of the Royal-Society of London (1667) was the first account of the Society and a manifesto for the plain, factual prose style that the new philosophy demanded.
biography: Born 1635 (baptised) at Henstridge, Dorset, educated at Wadham College, Oxford (Fellow), where he joined Wilkins's circle. He wrote a Pindaric ode on Cromwell (1659) and served as a chaplain and preacher after the Restoration. At the request of the Royal Society he composed its History (1667), celebrating its method and advocating a 'close, naked, natural way of speaking'. He rose in the church to become Dean of Westminster (1683) and Bishop of Rochester (1684), and was involved in the politics of James II's reign and the Revolution. He died on 20 May 1713.
literary_profile: The apologist and historian of the Royal Society whose prose ideal — plain, precise, free of rhetorical 'swelling' — became the manifesto for the modern scientific and plain style.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, expository, persuasive prose; historical narrative of an institution; advocacy of the plain style; and occasional Pindaric verse.
intellectual_concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institution; the reform of language toward the plain style; the reconciliation of science and religion; and public and ecclesiastical affairs.
historical_significance: Sprat's History of the Royal-Society is the foundational document of the Society's early ideals and the classic statement of the plain-style programme, widely quoted in the history of science and of English prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Sprat's birth year is approximate; his ecclesiastical and political career is documented, and his History is partly propagandistic for the Society's ideals.

literary_identity: Natural philosopher, inventor, and microscopist; his Micrographia (1665), with its spectacular engravings of the flea, the louse, and plant cells (he coined the word 'cell'), was a landmark of scientific illustration and of the literature of discovery.
biography: Born 18 July 1635 at Freshwater, Isle of Wight; educated at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became assistant to Boyle (building the air pump) and later Professor of Geometry. A founder-member and Curator of Experiments to the Royal Society, he published Micrographia (1665), a sensational success, and made contributions across physics (Hooke's law of elasticity), astronomy, geology, and architecture (as Surveyor to the City of London after the Great Fire, working with Wren). He disputed priority with Newton over optics and gravitation. He died on 3 March 1703; no certain portrait of him survives.
literary_profile: The brilliant experimentalist and observer whose Micrographia opened an invisible world to readers through its prose descriptions and magnificent engravings, inspiring wonder and the new empirical vision.
stylistic_characteristics: Descriptive, observational scientific prose; detailed accounts of apparatus and experiments; spectacular engraving and visual rhetoric; and a plain, empirical style.
intellectual_concerns: Microscopy and the structure of matter; experimental method and instrumentation; elasticity, light, and mechanics; geology and fossils; and architecture and rebuilding.
historical_significance: Micrographia is a founding work of microscopy and scientific illustration and influenced the literature and imagination of the new science (Pepys called it 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'); Hooke's wide contributions made him a central figure of the Royal Society.
biographical_uncertainty: Hooke's life is documented through Royal Society records and his diary; the destruction of his papers and the absence of a portrait have left his appearance and some achievements obscure.

literary_identity: The leading Cambridge Platonist; a poet-philosopher who defended a rational, spiritual Christianity against materialism and atheism, and who corresponded with Descartes and Anne Conway while writing philosophical and mystical treatises in verse and prose.
biography: Born 12 October 1614 at Grantham, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow (1639) and remained for life, declining preferment. He corresponded with Descartes (1648–49) and was the philosophical mentor of Anne Conway. His works include the Philosophical Poems (1647, including the 'Psychozoia' and 'Antipsychopannychia'), An Antidote Against Atheism (1653), Enthusiasmus Triumphatus (1656), and the Enchiridion Metaphysicum (1671), which argued against Cartesian mechanism and for the reality of spirit, extension, and the 'boniform faculty'. He defended belief in spirits and apparitions and died on 1 September 1687.
literary_profile: The Platonic philosopher-theologian who sought to reconcile reason, religion, and the new philosophy, opposing Hobbesian and Cartesian materialism with a spiritual, emanative metaphysics expressed in both verse and prose.
stylistic_characteristics: Philosophical verse (Spenserian stanzas) and prose; Platonic and mystical argument; a serene, speculative, sometimes visionary style; and polemic against atheism and 'enthusiasm'.
intellectual_concerns: The existence and nature of spirit and God; reason and religion; the critique of materialism and of religious 'enthusiasm'; the immortality of the soul; and the relation of Descartes to Platonism.
historical_significance: More was the central figure of Cambridge Platonism, influencing Conway, Glanvill, and later Latitudinarian and Romantic thought; his correspondence with Descartes is a key document of seventeenth-century philosophy.
biographical_uncertainty: More's life is documented through his works, correspondence, and a contemporary biography; his philosophical positions evolved and some attributions of influence are interpretive.

literary_identity: Cambridge Platonist philosopher and theologian; his vast True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678) argued against atheism and materialism for a rational, divinely ordered cosmos and an innate moral sense, a major work of seventeenth-century philosophy.
biography: Born 1617 at Aller, Somerset, educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where he became Master (1654) and a leading figure of the Platonic circle. He served as Regius Professor of Hebrew, held livings, and was a correspondent of Temple's and an influential university figure (he tutored William Temple). His magnum opus, The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), the first part of a projected larger work, refuted 'atheism' through erudite argument and posited 'plastic natures' and innate moral ideas. Posthumous treatises on morality (A Treatise Concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality, 1731) were published later. He died on 26 February 1688.
literary_profile: The learned metaphysician whose encyclopaedic, erudite arguments for a rational, moral, divinely ordered universe represent the philosophical summit of Cambridge Platonism.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, erudite, argumentative prose; massive learning and citation; philosophical and theological reasoning; and a systematic, cumulative method.
intellectual_concerns: The existence of God and the refutation of atheism; the true intellectual system of the universe; innate moral ideas and eternal morality; free will; and 'plastic natures' as a middle principle.
historical_significance: Cudworth's True Intellectual System was a major philosophical work that influenced later thinkers (including Shaftesbury and the moral-sense school) and stands as the most systematic statement of Cambridge Platonist metaphysics and ethics.
biographical_uncertainty: Cudworth's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through university and church records; much of his planned oeuvre was left unfinished or published posthumously.

literary_identity: Political philosopher; author of The Commonwealth of Oceana (1656), an influential republican utopia that argued government follows the distribution of property and prescribed a balanced constitution, shaping Whig and American republican thought.
biography: Born 3 January 1611 at Upton, Northamptonshire, educated at Trinity College, Oxford and the Middle Temple, travelling widely in Europe. He served as a groom of the bedchamber to Charles I (1647), remaining loyal in person while arguing republican principles, and was much affected by the king's execution. Imprisoned briefly, he published Oceana (1656), dedicated — provocatively — to Cromwell, arguing that political power rests on the 'balance' of landed property and proposing an ideal mixed republic with rotation of office and a secret ballot. He wrote further republican tracts (The Prerogative of Popular Government, 1658) and, after the Restoration, was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and died, broken in health, on 11 September 1677.
literary_profile: The republican theorist whose materialist analysis of power and property and whose constitutional utopia Oceana provided a durable vocabulary of republicanism for the English and American revolutions.
stylistic_characteristics: Argumentative political prose and utopian fiction; historical and classical analogy; constitutional scheming; and a dense, sometimes obscure, learned style.
intellectual_concerns: Republicanism and the balance of property; constitutional design, rotation, and the ballot; the rise and fall of states; civic virtue; and the critique of monarchy and of Hobbes.
historical_significance: Oceana profoundly influenced later republican and Whig thought, the 'country' ideology of the eighteenth century, and the American founders (Jefferson and Adams drew on Harrington's ideas of property, rotation, and the balanced constitution).
biographical_uncertainty: Harrington's life is documented but his later imprisonment and decline are partly anecdotal; the reception of Oceana was shaped by its dedication to Cromwell and its suppression.

literary_identity: Digger (True Leveller) leader and radical pamphleteer; his tracts — The New Law of Righteousness (1649) and The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652) — argued for communal cultivation of the land and an agrarian communism grounded in reason and the inner light.
biography: Born c. 1609 at Wigan, Lancashire, son of a merchant; he worked as a cloth merchant in London before being bankrupted by the Civil Wars. In 1649 he led the 'Diggers' in communally cultivating St George's Hill and other commons in Surrey, publishing pamphlets defending the action against landlords and the state. Suppressed by local opposition and the authorities, the movement collapsed by 1650. His fullest statement, The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652), dedicated to Cromwell, set out a communist commonwealth governed by reason and law. Little is known of his later life; he may have become a Quaker and died c. 1676.
literary_profile: The visionary radical whose prophetic, plain-style pamphlets argued that true freedom requires common ownership of the earth and the abolition of wage labour, grounding communism in reason, scripture, and the 'inner light'.
stylistic_characteristics: Urgent, prophetic, plain-style pamphlet prose; scriptural and rationalist argument; dialogue and declaration; and a direct, popular address.
intellectual_concerns: Common ownership and agrarian communism; the rights of the poor and the commons; reason, the inner light, and true religion; the critique of private property, law, and clergy; and popular sovereignty.
historical_significance: Winstanley is the foremost theorist of the Diggers and an early exponent of agrarian socialism and communism; his tracts are foundational documents of English radicalism and have been central to Marxist and libertarian-socialist readings of the English Revolution.
biographical_uncertainty: Winstanley's life after 1652 is very poorly documented; his birth and death dates are approximate and his later Quakerism is conjectural.

literary_identity: Leveller leader and pamphleteer; 'Freeborn John', whose tracts and trials demanded popular sovereignty, extended suffrage, and the legal rights of the 'freeborn Englishman', making him a founding figure of English radical and constitutional argument.
biography: Born c. 1614–15, probably at Greenwich, Kent; apprenticed to a London clothier and drawn to Puritan dissent. Imprisoned by Star Chamber (1638) for distributing unlicensed books, he was whipped and pilloried but defied the court, refusing to incriminate himself — a landmark for the right against self-incrimination. He fought for Parliament in the Civil Wars, then turned against the Grandees, co-authoring Leveller petitions and The Agreement of the People and repeatedly publishing tracts demanding legal rights and popular sovereignty. Repeatedly imprisoned by both Royalists and Parliament/Cromwell, he briefly became a Quaker before his death on 29 August 1657.
literary_profile: The tireless polemicist of the 'freeborn' rights of Englishmen, whose pamphlets and courtroom defiance advanced principles of due process, self-incrimination, and popular consent that echo in modern constitutional law.
stylistic_characteristics: Forceful, plain, popular polemic; legal and scriptural argument; petitions, tracts, and declarations; and a combative, self-justifying, energetic prose.
intellectual_concerns: Popular sovereignty and suffrage; the rights of the freeborn Englishman; legal process, self-incrimination, and imprisonment; the Leveller programme; and resistance to arbitrary power.
historical_significance: Lilburne and the Levellers produced the earliest sustained English arguments for democracy and legal rights; his defence against self-incrimination influenced the development of due process and the Fifth Amendment, and his tracts are foundational to radical constitutionalism.
major_influences: English common law and the Petition of Right
biographical_uncertainty: Lilburne's birth year and birthplace are uncertain; his voluminous pamphlets and trials are well documented, though his shifting allegiances complicate his record.

literary_identity: Latitudinarian divine and Archbishop of Canterbury; the most influential preacher of the late seventeenth century, whose clear, reasonable, moral sermons defined Anglican pulpit prose and the ideal of a tolerant, rational Christianity.
biography: Born 1630 at Sowerby, Yorkshire, educated at Clare Hall, Cambridge (Fellow). A Puritan by upbringing, he conformed at the Restoration, held preferment, and became Dean of St Paul's (1664) and a leading latitudinarian preacher. He supported the Revolution of 1688, was made Archbishop of Canterbury (1691) under William III, and worked for comprehension and toleration. His sermons — reasonable, moral, and elegantly plain — were immensely popular and widely published (posthumous collected volumes 1695–1704). He died on 22 November 1694.
literary_profile: The model Latitudinarian preacher, whose sermons argued for a reasonable, benevolent, practical Christianity in a lucid, classical prose that set the standard for Augustan pulpit and essay style.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, plain, elegant, well-reasoned prose; the moral sermon of practical divinity; classical balance and lucidity; and an irenic, moderate tone.
intellectual_concerns: Reasonable religion and natural theology; morality and practical Christianity; toleration and comprehension; the relation of reason and revelation; and the church's public role.
historical_significance: Tillotson's sermons were among the most read prose of the age, shaping Anglican latitudinarianism, the plain prose style, and eighteenth-century moral and religious writing (admired by Addison, Swift, and Johnson).
biographical_uncertainty: Tillotson's birth year is approximate; his life and sermons are well documented, and his posthumous publications were edited by others.

literary_identity: Scottish-born Anglican bishop, historian, and memoirist; author of the History of the Reformation of the Church of England (1679–1715) and the posthumous History of His Own Time, whose vivid, opinionated accounts are primary sources for the politics and religion of the era.
biography: Born 2 September 1643 in Edinburgh, educated at the University of Aberdeen and in Holland; ordained in the Scottish church, he travelled and preached widely, becoming a moderate latitudinarian and a chaplain to Charles II. He fell from favour, went into exile after the accession of James II (1685), and supported William of Orange, becoming Bishop of Salisbury (1689) and a leading Whig churchman. His History of the Reformation (in parts, 1679–1715) won him fame (and a doctorate from Oxford); his memoir, History of His Own Time, was published posthumously (1724–34). He had attended the deathbed of the Earl of Rochester (1680), which he recorded. He died on 17 March 1715.
literary_profile: The busy, partisan, and readable bishop-historian whose histories and memoir give a vivid, if biased, first-hand account of the Reformation, the Restoration, and the Revolution.
stylistic_characteristics: Lively, discursive, opinionated historical prose; memoir and eyewitness reportage; a plain, energetic style; and polemical digression.
intellectual_concerns: Church history and the Reformation; the politics and religion of Restoration and Revolution England; latitudinarianism and toleration; and the defence of the Protestant succession.
historical_significance: Burnet's History of the Reformation and History of His Own Time are indispensable (if partisan) sources for the period; his memoirs of Rochester's conversion and of the Whig churchmen illuminate the religious politics of the age.
biographical_uncertainty: Burnet's life is well documented through his own writings; his histories are avowedly partisan and require critical use, and the History of His Own Time was edited and published posthumously.

literary_identity: Translator, poet, and memoirist; the first person to translate the complete Lucretius into English (De Rerum Natura, c. 1650s), author of the Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson, and of the biblical epic Order and Disorder — a major, recently recovered woman writer of the Interregnum.
biography: Born January 1620 in the Tower of London, where her father was Lieutenant; unusually well educated alongside her brothers, she showed precocious talent in languages. She married the Puritan Colonel John Hutchinson (1638), governor of Nottingham during the Civil Wars, and after his death in royalist captivity (1664) wrote his Memoirs — a classic of biography and of Civil War history. She also translated Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (presented to the Earl of Anglesey, c. 1675; she later repudiated it on religious grounds) and wrote the verse epic Order and Disorder (only a canto was published in 1679; the full text recovered from manuscript in the twentieth century), as well as theological and elegiac verse. She died in 1681 at Owthorpe, Nottinghamshire.
literary_profile: The learned Puritan woman writer whose biography, epic, and translation display remarkable erudition and literary ambition, and whose work offers a woman's republican and religious perspective on the Civil Wars.
stylistic_characteristics: Eloquent biographical and historical prose; philosophical translation in verse; biblical epic; and elegiac and devotional poetry of intellectual depth.
intellectual_concerns: Puritan and republican politics; the Civil Wars and her husband's career; Lucretian atomism and its reconciliation with faith; biblical narrative and providence; and grief and memory.
historical_significance: Hutchinson's Memoirs are a primary source for the Civil Wars and a landmark of English biography; her Lucretius translation and Order and Disorder make her a major figure in the recovery of early modern women's writing and of the period's engagement with Epicureanism.
biographical_uncertainty: Hutchinson's life is documented through her own writings and family papers; much of her work was unpublished in her lifetime and recovered from manuscript, so dating and textual questions remain.
